# Responsible NLP Research Checklist

> For EMNLP 2026 via ACL Rolling Review (May 2026 cycle).
> Paper: "Depth Profiling: Classifying Recursive Generation Depth in Base LLM Text Chains"
>
> Instructions: For each question, answer Yes/No/N/A and provide section number (if Yes) or justification (if No).
> Not answering positively is NOT grounds for rejection. Incorrect/misleading answers CAN trigger desk rejection.

---

## A. For every submission

### A1. Did you discuss the *limitations* of your work?

**Yes.** §Limitations (after Conclusion, before References).

Key limitations discussed: (1) restricted to base models, instruction-tuned models degrade substantially (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1=0.338 vs 0.763 base); (2) generators tested up to 8.2B parameters, frontier 70B+ models untested; (3) prompt-type dependent performance (continuation 0.781 vs paraphrastic 0.671); (4) temperature sensitivity, reliable at t<=0.7 but degrades at t=0.9; (5) English-only; (6) 3-class granularity is practical ceiling (5-class F1~0.50); (7) reference model fixed to Pythia-410M (cross-reference spread 0.013).

### A2. Did you discuss any potential *risks* of your work?

**Yes.** §Ethics Statement.

Risks discussed: (1) depth estimation tools could be misused to suppress legitimate AI-generated content (e.g., accessibility tools, assistive writing); (2) method estimates depth not author identity, privacy implications minimal; (3) recommended for provenance transparency rather than content removal.

### A3. Do the abstract and introduction summarize the paper's main claims?

**Yes.** §Abstract, §1 (Introduction).

Abstract states: DDR binary partition finding, 7-feature ensemble binary F1=0.694 under LOGO, instruction-tuning limitation. Introduction (§1) details DDR binary partition with effect sizes, cross-generator generalization, and positions the contribution as task formulation + DDR analysis + classification pipeline.

---

## B. Did you use or create *scientific artifacts*?

**Yes.**

### B1. Did you cite the creators of artifacts you used?

**Yes.** §3 (Method), §2 (Related Work), §Ethics Statement.

All models cited with original papers: Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023), OLMo (Groeneveld et al., 2024), Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023). All baseline methods cited: FastDetectGPT (Bao et al., 2024), Binoculars (Hans et al., 2024), LD-Score, Avg-LogProb. Software: XGBoost, scikit-learn, PyTorch, Transformers (versions in Ethics Statement).

### B2. Did you discuss the *license or terms* for use and/or distribution of any artifacts?

**Yes.** §Ethics Statement, paragraph "Licenses."

Apache 2.0 (Pythia, OLMo, Mistral), Qwen License (Qwen3), Llama Community License (Llama 3.2), CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikipedia seeds). Our dataset and code will be released upon publication.

### B3. Did you discuss if your use of existing artifact(s) was consistent with their *intended use*?

**Yes.** §3 (Method), §Ethics Statement.

All models used for text generation, which is their intended use. Wikipedia used as seed text (publicly available encyclopedic content, consistent with CC BY-SA license). Our derived dataset is for research purposes only, compatible with original access conditions.

### B4. Did you discuss the steps taken to check whether the data contains any *information that names or uniquely identifies individual people* or *offensive content*?

**Yes.** §Ethics Statement.

Seed texts are Wikipedia excerpts (publicly available encyclopedic content). Generated texts are model continuations of these seeds. No personal data collection or annotation involving human subjects. Wikipedia content is editorially curated. We did not perform additional filtering for offensive content in model outputs as the texts are used for statistical feature extraction, not for public display or deployment.

### B5. Did you provide documentation of the artifacts (domains, languages, linguistic phenomena, demographic groups, etc.)?

**Yes.** §3.2 (Data Construction), Appendix A (Dataset Statistics).

Documentation includes: domain (English Wikipedia), language (English), generation parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus p=0.9, max 256 tokens), per-generator text counts, depth distribution, chain break statistics, token-level statistics.

### B6. Did you report relevant statistics (number of examples, train/test/dev splits, etc.)?

**Yes.** §3.2, §3.4 (Evaluation Protocol), Appendix A.

Total texts: 37,058. Chain breaks removed: 2,746. Short passages removed: 11. Per-generator and per-depth breakdowns in Appendix A. Evaluation uses Leave-One-Generator-Out (LOGO) cross-validation (no fixed train/test split; each fold holds out one generator as test).

---

## C. Did you run *computational experiments*?

**Yes.**

### C1. Did you report the *number of parameters* in the models used, the *total computational budget* (e.g., GPU hours), and *computing infrastructure* used?

**Yes.** Table 1 (parameter counts for all 8 generators: 0.6B to 8.2B), §3.2 (Pythia-410M reference model), §Ethics Statement paragraph "Compute budget" (4x NVIDIA RTX 5090 32GB, ~62 GPU-hours total).

### C2. Did you discuss the experimental setup, including *hyperparameter search* and *best-found hyperparameter* values?

**Yes.** §3.4 (Evaluation Protocol), Appendix C (Classifier Sensitivity).

XGBoost uses standard defaults without hyperparameter search: n_estimators=200, max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.1. Justification: Appendix C demonstrates that four alternative classifiers (CORAL, CORN, Frank-Hall ordinal methods, standard MLP) yield comparable performance (F1 range 0.669-0.696), confirming discriminative power resides in features, not classifier tuning. Stability: LOGO F1 std < 0.001 over 5 random seeds.

### C3. Did you report *descriptive statistics* about your results (error bars, summary statistics), and is it transparent whether you are reporting max, mean, etc.?

**Yes.** §4 (Results), Tables 1-2.

All primary results include 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (n=1,000 resamples). McNemar tests for pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction within test families (§3.4). Cohen's d effect sizes for DDR partition (§4.2). Results are mean LOGO F1 across folds (explicitly stated). Per-generator breakdowns provide full distribution visibility.

### C4. If you used existing packages, did you report the implementation, model, and parameter settings used?

**Yes.** §Ethics Statement paragraph "Software."

Python 3.12.3, PyTorch 2.10.0 (CUDA 12.8), Transformers 4.57.6, XGBoost 3.2.0, scikit-learn 1.8.0, NumPy 2.2.6, pandas 3.0.2, SciPy 1.17.1. Generation parameters: temperature 0.7, nucleus p=0.9, max_new_tokens=256 (§3.2).

---

## D. Did you use *human annotators* (e.g., crowdworkers) or *research with human subjects*?

**No.** All labels are automatically determined by the generation chain construction process (depth = position in the iterative generation chain). No human annotation, crowdsourcing, or human subjects research was conducted.

*(D1-D5 skipped per checklist instructions.)*

---

## E. Did you use *AI assistants* (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot) in your research, coding, or writing?

**Yes.**

### E1. Did you include information about your use of AI assistants?

**Yes.** §Acknowledgements (to be added in camera-ready).

Claude Code (Anthropic) was used for coding assistance (experiment scripts, data processing pipelines) and writing assistance (language polishing, LaTeX formatting). All outputs were verified by the authors for correctness. The AI assistant was not used for generating scientific claims, experimental design decisions, or result interpretation. All authors take full responsibility for the content.

# ARR Responsible NLP Research Checklist

> For EMNLP 2026 via ACL Rolling Review. Answers reference specific paper sections.

---

## Section A: Did you describe the limitations of your work?

**A1. Did you describe the limitations of your work?**
Yes. See the dedicated Limitations section (§Limitations, after Conclusion). Key limitations discussed:

**A3. Do your abstract and introduction summarize the paper's main claims?**

Introduction (§1) details the DDR binary partition with effect sizes, cross-generator generalization, and positions the contribution as task formulation + DDR analysis.

---

## Section B: Did you use or create scientific artifacts?

**B1. Did you cite the creators of artifacts you used?**
Yes. All models cited: Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023), OLMo (Groeneveld et al., 2024), Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023). All baseline methods cited: FastDetectGPT, Binoculars, LD-Score, Avg-LogProb. Software versions listed in Ethics Statement.

**B2. Did you discuss the license or terms for use and/or distribution of any artifacts?**
Yes. Ethics Statement §Licenses: Apache 2.0 (Pythia, OLMo, Mistral), Qwen License (Qwen3), Llama Community License (Llama 3.2), CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikipedia seeds).

**B3. Did you discuss if your use of existing artifacts is consistent with their intended use?**
Yes. All models used for text generation (intended use). Wikipedia used as seed text (public domain content).

**B4. Did you discuss the steps taken to check whether the data/models contain information that names or uniquely identifies people or offensive content?**
Partially. Seed texts are Wikipedia excerpts (publicly available encyclopedic content). Generated text is model output conditioned on these seeds. No personal data collection or annotation involving human subjects.

**B5. Did you provide documentation of the artifacts?**
Yes. §3 (Method) fully documents: generation chain construction, feature extraction pipeline, evaluation protocol. Appendix provides dataset statistics (Appendix A), per-generator breakdowns, and ablation details. Code/data/models will be released upon publication.

---

## Section C: Did you run computational experiments?

**C1. Did you report the number of parameters in each model used?**
Yes. Table 1 lists parameter counts for all 8 generators (0.6B to 8.2B). Reference model: Pythia-410M (410M parameters). §3.2 specifies exact model identifiers.

**C2. Did you report the computing infrastructure used?**
Yes. Ethics Statement §Compute budget: 4× NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs (32GB each), approximately 62 GPU-hours total.

**C3. Did you report the average runtime for each approach?**
Partially. Table 2 reports inference time per text (ms/text): 7-feature ensemble 9.7ms, 4-detector ensemble 22.8ms. Training time not separately reported (XGBoost training is negligible, <1min per fold).

**C4. Did you report the evaluation metrics, along with the values and confidence intervals?**
Yes. All primary results include 95% bootstrap CIs (n=1000). Tables 1-2 report CIs. McNemar tests for pairwise comparisons (§4.2). Bonferroni correction applied within test families (§3.4). Cohen's d effect sizes reported for DDR partition (§4.2).

**C6. Did you report the number and range of values tried for each hyperparameter?**
N/A. No hyperparameter search conducted; default XGBoost parameters used throughout. Stability confirmed: LOGO F1 std < 0.001 over 5 random seeds (§3.4).

---

## Section D: Did you use or create data?

**D1. Did you discuss how the data was collected or created?**
Yes. §3.2 describes chain construction: ~1000 Wikipedia seed passages per generator, iterative continuation with fixed prompt template, temperature 0.7, nucleus p=0.9, max 256 tokens. 37,058 texts after removing 2,746 chain breaks and 11 short passages. Appendix A provides full dataset statistics.

**D2. Did you report the basic statistics of the data used?**
Yes. §3.2: total texts (37,058), chain breaks (2,746), depth distribution. Appendix A: per-generator breakdown, depth-class counts, token statistics.

**D3. Did you discuss if the data you are using/creating contains personally identifiable information or offensive content?**
Yes. Ethics Statement: "All texts analyzed are LLM-generated from publicly available Wikipedia seeds; no personal or sensitive data is involved."

**D4. Did you provide the data?**
Will release upon publication. Ethics Statement: "All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication."

---

## Section E: Did you use human annotators or crowdworkers?

**E1-E5.** N/A. No human annotation or crowdsourcing was used. All labels are automatically determined by the generation chain construction process (depth = position in the chain).

\subsection*{Data-Driven Clustering}

To assess the DDR partition structure and determine whether the drifting/non-drifting split is data-driven, we apply $k$-means clustering ($k \in \{2,3,4,5\}$) to the seven features in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space (Table~\ref{tab:clustering}).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{$k$-means clustering of 7 features in $(|\rho|, d)$ space.}
\label{tab:clustering}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{ccp{5.5cm}}
\toprule
$k$ & Silhouette & Clusters \\
\midrule
2 & \textbf{0.632} & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} \\
3 & 0.499 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
4 & 0.571 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632) is the strongest cluster structure.
At $k{=}3$, entropy min forms its own cluster rather than joining the near-stationary group because its pooled $|\rho|{=}0.40$ (driven by the gen-0/gen-1 boundary) places it far from other near-stationary features in $\rho$ space.
The 3/1/3 DDR partition resolves this by using the gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ Cohen's $d$ ($d{=}0.03$) to place entropy min in the near-stationary group, a domain-informed refinement that unsupervised clustering cannot recover from pooled statistics alone.
At $k{=}4$ (silhouette\,=\,0.571), entropy std separates from the near-stationary group, consistent with its intermediate DDR classification.

\subsection*{TOST Equivalence Bound Sensitivity}
\label{app:tost-sensitivity}

Table~\ref{tab:tost-sensitivity} shows the fraction of generators for which each feature passes the TOST equivalence test (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $\alpha{=}0.05$) at three equivalence bounds $\varepsilon$.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{TOST equivalence pass rate across 8 generators at varying $\varepsilon$.}
\label{tab:tost-sensitivity}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.15}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.20}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.25}$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
 & TTR & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 7/8 & 8/8 & 8/8 \\
 & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 6/8 & 6/8 & 6/8 \\
 & tail decay & 4/8 & 4/8 & 7/8 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The partition is robust to the equivalence bound: drifting features reject equivalence at all $\varepsilon$ for all generators, while entropy min passes even at the stricter bound $\varepsilon{=}0.15$ (7/8 generators).
Tail decay is the most $\varepsilon$-sensitive near-stationary feature, passing 4/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.20$ but 7/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.25$; the four non-passing generators show $|d|{=}0.15$--$0.22$, still well below the drifting threshold ($d > 0.50$).
Entropy max is stable across all three bounds (6/8), with the two failures (Pythia-1B $d{=}0.21$, Pythia-2.8B $d{=}0.25$) reflecting same-family reference affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model.

\paragraph{Partition stability across $\varepsilon$ thresholds.}
\label{app:epsilon-sweep}

The DDR partition classifies features as non-stationary ($d \geq \varepsilon$) or stationary ($d < \varepsilon$) based on pooled Cohen's $d$ (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Table~\ref{tab:epsilon-sweep} reports the critical $\varepsilon$ at which each feature's classification changes; the three drifting and three near-stationary features maintain their classification for all $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Partition stability under varying $\varepsilon$. Critical threshold: the $\varepsilon$ above which a feature is reclassified as stationary. The drifting/near-stationary split is invariant for $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$; only entropy std ($d{=}0.55$) changes at $\varepsilon > 0.55$.}
\label{tab:epsilon-sweep}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Pooled $d$} & \textbf{Stationary at $\varepsilon >$} \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 1.17 & 1.17 \\
 & TTR & 0.88 & 0.88 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0.76 & 0.76 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.55 & 0.55 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 0.08 & 0.08 \\
 & tail decay & 0.08 & 0.08 \\
 & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 0.016 & 0.016 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\noindent The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$: the three drifting features remain non-stationary at all $\varepsilon < 0.76$, the three near-stationary features remain stationary at all $\varepsilon > 0.08$, and only entropy std changes classification (becoming stationary at $\varepsilon > 0.55$), confirming it as the sole threshold-sensitive feature.
The minimum gap between adjacent zone boundaries ($d_{\text{hapax}} - d_{\sigma_H} = 0.21$) exceeds typical effect-size estimation uncertainty, providing a margin against sampling noise.

\subsection*{Holdout Generator Split Validation}
\label{app:holdout-split}

To confirm the DDR partition is not an artifact of the specific generator pool, we split the eight generators into disjoint selection (4) and validation (4) sets, compute per-subset pooled $(|\rho|, d)$, and check whether all seven features receive the same zone assignment in both subsets.
We evaluate two complementary splits to avoid dependence on a single partition:
Split~A selects \{Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B, Llama);
Split~B selects \{Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, Llama).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Holdout split validation of the DDR partition. Selection (sel) and validation (val) $|\rho|$ and $d$ for two disjoint 4/4 generator splits. Zone assignment is identical across all four subsets for every feature.}
\label{tab:holdout-split}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcccccc}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Split A}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Split B}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-8}
\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & sel $|\rho|$ & val $|\rho|$ & $\Delta|\rho|$ & sel $|\rho|$ & val $|\rho|$ & $\Delta|\rho|$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0.60 & 0.58 & 0.02 & 0.60 & 0.58 & 0.02 \\
 & TTR & 0.61 & 0.59 & 0.02 & 0.60 & 0.59 & 0.01 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0.62 & 0.60 & 0.02 & 0.62 & 0.61 & 0.01 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.19 & 0.21 & 0.02 & 0.22 & 0.17 & 0.05 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 0.39 & 0.36 & 0.03 & 0.38 & 0.37 & 0.01 \\
 & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 0.05 & 0.05 & 0.00 & 0.04 & 0.06 & 0.02 \\
 & tail decay & 0.10 & 0.08 & 0.02 & 0.11 & 0.07 & 0.04 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Under simple joint $(|\rho|, d)$ thresholds, both splits produce a 3/2/2 partition: entropy min is classified as a second intermediate feature due to its elevated pooled $|\rho|$ (0.36--0.39).
However, entropy min's binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) $d$ values are uniformly below 0.06 across all four split${\times}$subset combinations, consistent with near-stationarity on the task-relevant metric; its pooled $|\rho|$ reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary rather than sustained drift.
Five of seven features are unambiguously classified under any reasonable criterion; entropy min's boundary status is resolved by the binary-task $d$ criterion.

Selection and validation subsets produce identical partitions in both splits (Table~\ref{tab:holdout-split}; Figure~\ref{fig:holdout-scatter}).
The maximum $\Delta|\rho|$ between selection and validation is 0.05 (entropy std, Split~B), and the minimum gap between adjacent zones remains $>$0.15 in all subsets.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig_ddr_holdout_split.pdf}
\caption{Holdout split validation in $(|\rho|, d)$ space. Filled markers: selection set; hollow: validation set. Zone assignments are identical across subsets; selection/validation pairs cluster tightly for all features.}
\label{fig:holdout-scatter}
\end{figure}

\subsection*{Heteroscedasticity Sensitivity}
\label{app:heteroscedasticity}

Levene tests reject equal variance between gen-1 and gen-2+ for drifting features ($p < 10^{-10}$; variance ratios 1.86--2.21).
To verify that the DDR partition is robust to this heteroscedasticity, we supplement pooled Cohen's $d$ with Glass's $\Delta$ (using the gen-1 standard deviation as denominator) and Cliff's $\delta$ (a non-parametric ordinal effect size; Table~\ref{tab:effect-sizes}).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Effect size comparison (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $N$\,=\,29{,}095). Glass's $\Delta$ uses the gen-1 SD as denominator; Cliff's $\delta$ thresholds follow Romano et al.\ (2006): $|\delta| < 0.147$ negligible, $< 0.33$ small, $< 0.474$ medium, otherwise large.}
\label{tab:effect-sizes}
\begin{tabular}{llrrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{$|d|$} & \textbf{$|\Delta|$} & \textbf{$|\delta|$} \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & ent.\ mean & 1.054 & 1.410 & 0.587 \\

\midrule
Intermediate & ent.\ std & 0.457 & 0.605 & 0.295 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & tail decay & 0.087 & 0.099 & 0.072 \\
 & ent.\ max & 0.062 & 0.065 & 0.021 \\

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\noindent Effect sizes in Table~\ref{tab:effect-sizes} are computed on the binary task (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+); the main text (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) reports 3-class pooled $d$ values (e.g., hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), which are slightly larger because the gen-0/gen-1 contrast contributes additional separation.
Glass's $\Delta$ amplifies drifting effects (1.41 vs.\ 1.05 for entropy mean) because gen-2+ variance exceeds gen-1 variance (ratio 2.08), making the pooled Cohen's $d$ conservative.
Near-stationary features remain negligible under both parametric metrics ($|\Delta| \leq 0.099$).
The minimum drifting-to-maximum-near-stationary gap is $9.5\times$ under Glass's $\Delta$ (0.936\,/\,0.099); heteroscedasticity does not erode the partition.
Cliff's $\delta$ classifies all drifting features as ``large'' ($|\delta| > 0.474$) and entropy std as ``small'' ($|\delta|{=}0.295$), consistent with the parametric partition.

\noindent $^{\dagger}$Entropy min's elevated Cliff's $\delta$ (0.354, ``medium'') reflects distributional shape asymmetry between gen-1 and gen-2+ that rank-based statistics detect but location measures do not (Cohen's $d{=}0.016$, Glass's $\Delta{=}0.015$).
This is consistent with its documented boundary status (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}): the gen-0/gen-1 transition produces rank-order shifts that persist into deeper generations without affecting the mean.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Existing AI text detection addresses a single question: is this text human or machine \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score}?
This binary framing is a blind spot.
As LLM outputs re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} and seed further generation, web text accumulates at varying recursive depths: an estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, each generation cycle producing text qualitatively different from both its human source and its first-generation predecessor.
Distinguishing these depths matters for data provenance \cite{ccnet,dsir} and model collapse theory \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}, but no current method addresses it.

We introduce \emph{depth fingerprinting}: classifying text by ordinal generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) and decomposing the distributional drift across depths into structurally distinct components.
The core finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): across eight base-model generators from five families (0.6B--8B), the NLL distribution's central tendency (mean entropy, lexical diversity) drifts monotonically with depth while its shape (entropy extremes, tail structure) remains an order of magnitude more stable ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$ vs.\ $d < 0.10$).
This location/shape asymmetry has analytical value independent of classification: it reveals that fixed-parameter autoregressive sampling systematically compresses distributional location while preserving higher-order structure, a pattern distinct from the tail-coverage erosion in model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion}.
Concurrent studies characterize convergence in paraphrastic and translation chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains}; ours is the first to decompose the drift mechanism and exploit the asymmetry for cross-generator depth prediction.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models to isolate generation dynamics from alignment artifacts (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

As a proof of concept, a 7-feature ensemble exploiting DDR achieves binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation and 0.830 on heterogeneous cross-model chains, exceeding individual detection baselines by 6.7--36.3\,pp at 2.4$\times$ lower inference cost than multi-detector ensembles that match its performance.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Analytical finding.} Data-driven clustering ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632) reveals that inference-chain drift decomposes into a drifting location component ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) and a stable shape component ($d < 0.10$ for the near-stationary core). Prior work documents \emph{what converges}; the novel observation is \emph{what is preserved}, enabling depth detection without per-generator calibration.
    \item \textbf{Task and evaluation suite.} We formulate generation depth classification and construct a dataset of 37K texts from eight generators spanning five model families (0.6B--8B), evaluated under leave-one-generator-out cross-validation.
    \item \textbf{Proof-of-concept depth classifier.} A 7-feature ensemble exploiting DDR achieves binary F1\,=\,0.830 on cross-model chains, with systematic boundary analysis across temperature, prompt type, instruction tuning, and downstream quality.
\end{enumerate}

 \subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
 \label{sec:related-detection}
 
-Methods for distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text have evolved from statistical tests \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies} to zero-shot reference-model approaches \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt} and learned classifiers \cite{feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}.

 \section{Introduction}
 \label{sec:introduction}
 
-Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text---estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}---and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
-The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
-Understanding the distributional properties of such recursive generation is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet the phenomenon itself---how distributional features evolve across generation depths---remains underexplored.
+Existing AI text detection addresses a single question: is this text human or machine \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score}?
+This binary framing is a blind spot.
+As LLM outputs re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} and seed further generation, web text accumulates at varying recursive depths: an estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, each generation cycle producing text qualitatively different from both its human source and its first-generation predecessor.
+Distinguishing these depths matters for data provenance \cite{ccnet,dsir} and model collapse theory \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}, but no current method addresses it.
 
-We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic generation chains under controlled conditions, using six base (pretrained) models from three families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen; 0.6B--8.2B parameters).
-We restrict to base models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds---output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping---that obscure the generation mechanism's intrinsic behavior.
-Preliminary experiments confirm this concern: instruct models show substantially degraded depth signal (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), motivating the controlled base-model setting as the appropriate starting point for isolating recursive drift phenomena.
+We introduce \emph{depth fingerprinting}: classifying text by ordinal generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) and decomposing the distributional drift across depths into structurally distinct components.
+The core finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): across eight base-model generators from five families (0.6B--8B), the NLL distribution's central tendency (mean entropy, lexical diversity) drifts monotonically with depth while its shape (entropy extremes, tail structure) remains an order of magnitude more stable ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$ vs.\ $d < 0.10$).
+This location/shape asymmetry has analytical value independent of classification: it reveals that fixed-parameter autoregressive sampling systematically compresses distributional location while preserving higher-order structure, a pattern distinct from the tail-coverage erosion in model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion}.
+Concurrent studies characterize convergence in paraphrastic and translation chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains}; ours is the first to decompose the drift mechanism and exploit the asymmetry for cross-generator depth prediction.
+We restrict to base (pretrained) models to isolate generation dynamics from alignment artifacts (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
 
-Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material.
-A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
-We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label---and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
-No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
-When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.81; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), making any single detector unreliable.
-Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; we study non-paraphrastic chains where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.
+As a proof of concept, a 7-feature ensemble exploiting DDR achieves binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation and 0.830 on heterogeneous cross-model chains, exceeding individual detection baselines by 6.7--36.3\,pp at 2.4$\times$ lower inference cost than multi-detector ensembles that match its performance.
 
-We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
-We hypothesize that this pattern reflects recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution while preserving its functional form: the sampling mechanism determines distributional shape regardless of input content.
-The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+).
-However, the strength of this signal is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains exhibit stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting chains (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
-
-We additionally report a negative finding: depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 vs.\ 2.387).
-
-Our contributions are:
+Our contributions:
 \begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
-    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive generation depths.
-    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across six base-model generators spanning three model families: a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 for leak-free depth discrimination, outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).
+    \item \textbf{Analytical finding.} Data-driven clustering ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632) reveals that inference-chain drift decomposes into a drifting location component ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) and a stable shape component ($d < 0.10$ for the near-stationary core). Prior work documents \emph{what converges}; the novel observation is \emph{what is preserved}, enabling depth detection without per-generator calibration.
+    \item \textbf{Task and evaluation suite.} We formulate generation depth classification and construct a dataset of 37K texts from eight generators spanning five model families (0.6B--8B), evaluated under leave-one-generator-out cross-validation.
+    \item \textbf{Proof-of-concept depth classifier.} A 7-feature ensemble exploiting DDR achieves binary F1\,=\,0.830 on cross-model chains, with systematic boundary analysis across temperature, prompt type, instruction tuning, and downstream quality.
 \end{enumerate}
-
-The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
-\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
-\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
-\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, and baseline comparisons.
-\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses mechanistic hypotheses and scope boundaries.

+We introduce \emph{depth fingerprinting}: classifying text by ordinal generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) and decomposing the distributional drift across depths into structurally distinct components.
+The core finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): across eight base-model generators from five families (0.6B--8B), the NLL distribution's central tendency (mean entropy, lexical diversity) drifts monotonically with depth while its shape (entropy extremes, tail structure) remains an order of magnitude more stable ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$ vs.\ $d < 0.10$).
+This location/shape asymmetry has analytical value independent of classification: it reveals that fixed-parameter autoregressive sampling systematically compresses distributional location while preserving higher-order structure, a pattern distinct from the tail-coverage erosion in model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion}.
+Concurrent studies characterize convergence in paraphrastic and translation chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains}; ours is the first to decompose the drift mechanism and exploit the asymmetry for cross-generator depth prediction.
+We restrict to base (pretrained) models to isolate generation dynamics from alignment artifacts (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

-A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
-We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label---and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
-No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.

+As a proof of concept, a 7-feature ensemble exploiting DDR achieves binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation and 0.830 on heterogeneous cross-model chains, exceeding individual detection baselines by 6.7--36.3\,pp at 2.4$\times$ lower inference cost than multi-detector ensembles that match its performance.
 
-We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.

-

-

 \begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
-    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive generation depths.
-    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across six base-model generators spanning three model families: a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 for leak-free depth discrimination, outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).

Prior work documents \emph{what converges}; the novel observation is \emph{what is preserved}, enabling depth detection without per-generator calibration.
+    \item \textbf{Task and evaluation suite.} We formulate generation depth classification and construct a dataset of 37K texts from eight generators spanning five model families (0.6B--8B), evaluated under leave-one-generator-out cross-validation.
+    \item \textbf{Proof-of-concept depth classifier.} A 7-feature ensemble exploiting DDR achieves binary F1\,=\,0.830 on cross-model chains, with systematic boundary analysis across temperature, prompt type, instruction tuning, and downstream quality.

-\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.

 \label{sec:results-differential}
 
-Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.
-This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution---the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts), while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant).

Thin lines: individual generators; bold black: cross-generator mean. This contrast defines the differential depth response (DDR).}

+This 2-way split is the data-driven core of DDR; higher $k$ degrades cluster quality ($k{=}3$: silhouette\,=\,0.499).

+Five independent effect-size metrics converge on the drifting/non-drifting partition, confirming the location/shape asymmetry reflects distributional structure rather than feature-selection artifact.

Per-gen std measures cross-generator consistency of the binary metric. The 7-feature ensemble is the strongest single-model method on both metrics and matches the best multi-detector ensemble on binary F1.}
+\caption{Depth classification (8-gen LOGO, pooled evaluation; slightly higher than per-generator macro average in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}). Identical XGBoost configuration. 7-feature: one 410M model (905\,MB); 4-det ensembles: two models, 1.4B params (2{,}868\,MB). Individual detection scores (N/A) share the reference-model forward pass; per-method timing is not separately profiled.}
 \label{tab:baselines}
 \end{table}
 
-The 7-feature ensemble achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723, outperforming every individual baseline ($p < 0.001$ for all; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).
-Combining all four detection scores into a 4-detector ensemble yields binary F1\,=\,0.712---below the 7-feature ensemble; adding surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) raises it to 0.724, matching the 7-feature ensemble and confirming that surface diversity features capture signal complementary to detection scores.
-The multi-detector 3-class advantage (0.796 vs.\ 0.789) is driven entirely by gen-0 classification; existing detectors do not capture the finer depth signal between gen-1 and gen-2+.
-
-
-\subsection{Downstream Utility}
-\label{sec:results-downstream}
+\begin{figure}[t]
+\centering
+\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_baseline_comparison.pdf}
+\caption{LOGO binary F1 vs.\ inference cost (8-gen pooled). The 7-feature ensemble matches multi-detector ensembles at 2.4$\times$ lower cost; individual detectors vary widely when repurposed for depth.}
+\label{fig:baseline-ci}
+\end{figure}
 
-Depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality.
-Fine-tuning OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) shows that data quantity dominates depth composition: random subsampling (ppl\,=\,2.367) outperforms depth-stratified selection (ppl\,=\,2.387) at equal sample count (Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}).
+The 7-feature ensemble exceeds all individual baselines in 3-class F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,6.7--36.3\,pp; Figure~\ref{fig:baseline-ci}) and the pure 4-detector ensemble in binary F1 (0.705 vs.\ 0.700).
+Adding DDR's two surface features to the four detectors yields the highest binary F1 (0.708), marginally above the 7-feature set at 2.4$\times$ inference cost.
+DDR's primary contribution is therefore not classification performance---where multi-detector ensembles match or marginally exceed it---but decomposing depth signal into location-sensitive and shape-stable components, a distinction absent from both binary detection methods and model collapse analyses (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
